title: An Anti-Inflammatory Diet Cut Dementia Risk by Up to 29% — Even in People Already Showing Alzheimer's Signs
excerpt: A 15-year study of nearly 2,000 older adults found that eating to cool inflammation helped the most in those whose blood already carried Alzheimer's biomarkers — and the foods that worked are staples of the Indian kitchen.
body:
The promise that food can protect the brain is not new. But a study just published in *JAMA Network Open* narrows the question in a way that matters: which kind of healthy diet helps, and does it help people who already show the earliest biological traces of Alzheimer's disease?

The answer, drawn from a 15-year follow-up of 1,865 Swedish adults aged 60 and older, is that an anti-inflammatory diet — measured by a scoring system called the reversed Empirical Dietary Inflammatory Index, or rEDII — was the only eating pattern that significantly lowered dementia risk in people whose blood already contained elevated Alzheimer's biomarkers such as p-tau 217, neurofilament light (NFL), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP).

The risk reduction was striking: **21 to 29 percent lower dementia risk**, depending on the biomarker examined.

## What the Study Actually Measured

Researchers at the Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm and the University of Ljubljana assessed adherence to three dietary patterns using a 98-item food frequency questionnaire completed by participants enrolled in the Swedish National study on Aging and Care in Kungsholmen (SNAC-K).

The three patterns were:

- **The Alternate Mediterranean Diet (AMED)** — rich in vegetables, fruits, legumes, nuts, whole grains, fish, and moderate alcohol, with limited red and processed meat.
- **The Alternative Healthy Eating Index (AHEI)** — a broader index of diet quality designed around chronic disease prevention.
- **The rEDII** — a scoring system that captures the inflammatory potential of a diet. Higher scores mean more vegetables, tea, coffee, and less red and processed meat, refined grains, and sugary drinks.

During the 15-year follow-up, 240 of the 1,865 participants developed dementia. Among those with elevated Alzheimer's biomarkers in their blood, only the rEDII — the anti-inflammatory diet — was linked to a significantly lower risk. The Mediterranean-style diet showed protective effects only in people whose biomarker levels were still low.

"Unlike the other two indices," said lead researcher Anja Mrhar, "the rEDII is based on how patterns of food intake have been associated with inflammatory markers in previous research. It therefore reflects a more specific inflammation-related dimension of diet quality."

## Why Inflammation Is the Key

Chronic inflammation is now understood to be both a driver and a consequence of Alzheimer's pathology. Amyloid beta plaques and tau tangles — the hallmarks of the disease — trigger inflammatory cascades in the brain that accelerate neuronal damage.

"There is mounting evidence to suggest that what happens in the body can influence inflammatory processes in the brain through the gut-brain-immune axis," said Emer MacSweeney, a consultant neuroradiologist at Re:Cognition Health who was not involved in the study. "It is therefore plausible that individuals who already have Alzheimer's-related changes may benefit most because reducing inflammatory burden could help slow some of the downstream processes that contribute to cognitive decline."

Oxidative stress — mainly arising from chronic inflammation — speeds up cellular aging and fuels chronic diseases including Alzheimer's, cancer, and Type 2 diabetes.

## The South Asian Connection

For the Indian diaspora, this research carries particular weight. South Asians have among the highest rates of Type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome in the world — conditions driven in large part by chronic systemic inflammation. The prevalence of diabetes among Indian Americans is roughly 23 percent, compared with about 12 percent for the general US population.

The encouraging news is that many staples of the traditional Indian kitchen already align with anti-inflammatory principles: turmeric (curcumin), dark leafy greens, legumes, whole grains, nuts, and seeds. The spice box of a typical South Indian or North Indian kitchen — with its turmeric, ginger, black pepper, cumin, and coriander — reads like a pharmacopoeia of anti-inflammatory compounds.

But the shift is happening in the wrong direction. Ultra-processed food consumption among Indian Americans and NRIs has risen sharply, particularly among second-generation households. Packaged snacks, sugary beverages, and refined grains — the exact foods that score poorly on the rEDII — are displacing the dal-sabzi-roti pattern that generations relied on.

## What to Eat — and What to Avoid

MacSweeney offered practical recommendations: "Increase consumption of leafy green vegetables, berries, oily fish, nuts, seeds, and whole grains, while reducing intake of highly processed foods, sugary drinks, and processed meats. Excess alcohol should also be avoided."

The researchers themselves were careful to note that this was an observational study. "The findings should not be overinterpreted," Mrhar cautioned. "They do not show that diet can prevent dementia, nor do they prove that changing diet after biomarker changes have emerged will alter disease progression."

But the signal is consistent with a growing body of evidence linking diet quality to brain health. A separate recent study found that the DASH diet — which emphasises fruits, vegetables, nuts, and low sodium — was associated with a 41 percent lower risk of subjective cognitive decline, outperforming even the Mediterranean diet.

"No single food or supplement has been proven to prevent dementia," MacSweeney said. "The overall quality and consistency of dietary habits over many years appear to matter most."

For families navigating the diaspora's dual food culture — where a morning of *idli-sambar* can give way to an afternoon of fast food — the message is not to abandon either world, but to lean into what the Indian kitchen has always done well: whole foods, spices, and meals cooked from scratch.
